analysis.one_liner: Imposes a 15 percent extra tax on corporate profits from Iraq war contracts.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it died in the Ways and Means Committee after being introduced by a single sponsor with no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would add a 15 percent surtax on the taxable income companies earn from U.S. government contracts specifically tied to the war in Iraq. It would not apply to pay earned by soldiers or other federal employees. The bill's findings point to large corporations making billions from the war, including over $2 billion in no-bid contracts to Halliburton, and say the tax follows precedents from World War II and Korea. The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers generally, because the tax would claw back a share of profits companies earned on Iraq war contracts, and the domestic programs the bill's findings say were being cut while contractors netted billions. Soldiers and federal employees are expressly excluded from the tax.

how_it_helps.text: Imposes an additional 15 percent tax on taxable income attributable to U.S. contracts specifically for goods or services for the war in Iraq [S2][S3].
The bill cites precedent for excess-profits taxes during World War II and the Korean War, framing the measure as recouping wartime windfalls [S3].

The bill's findings state that Halliburton and its subsidiaries received more than $2 billion from no-bid contracts, and that five large corporations benefited from the largest reconstruction project since World War II [S3].
Amounts received by members of the Armed Forces or other federal employees for their services are exempt from the tax [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Corporations earning income from U.S. contracts for the Iraq war, principally the large defense and reconstruction contractors named in the bill's findings: Halliburton, Bechtel Group, Fluor Corp, Parsons Corp, and the Louis Berger Group.

drawbacks.text: The bill raises the cost of doing business for Iraq war contractors, who could pass some of it back to the government through higher contract prices, partially offsetting the revenue gain.
The bill does not specify how the additional revenue would be used; its findings reference cuts to domestic programs but the text only imposes the tax [S3].

Determining which portion of a company's taxable income is 'attributable to' Iraq war contracts could be administratively difficult, especially under broadly worded contracts like the oil-infrastructure work the findings describe [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit to taxpayers is real but untested: a 15 percent surtax on contractor profits from Iraq contracts would shift billions, by the bill's own account, from large defense and reconstruction firms to the Treasury. The main costs are the risk of contractors recovering the tax through contract pricing and the difficulty of separating Iraq-related income from other business. The bill was never amended, debated, or costed, so its design was never refined.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on March 2, 2006, and the committee never took it up; it died there when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Rep. Major Owens introduced the Excess War Profits Act of 2006 in the House on March 2, 2006 [S1][S5].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day and received no further action [S5].
The 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007, without the bill ever leaving committee, receiving a hearing, or getting a floor vote [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The Iraq war contractors who would have paid the 15 percent surtax, particularly Halliburton and the other large reconstruction firms named in the bill's findings, kept their profits untaxed. Ways and Means members never had to take a position on the issue.

for.name: Rep. Major Owens
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Excess War Profits Act of 2006 and was its only sponsor.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on March 2, 2006 and never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill died in committee.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill had no cosponsors from either party, so there is no record of how members of either party would have lined up.

industries.industry: Defense and reconstruction contractors (Halliburton, Bechtel, Fluor, Parsons, Louis Berger)
industries.note: The bill would tax 15 percent of their income from Iraq war contracts, directly reducing profits the bill's findings say came largely from no-bid contracts and taxpayer-funded reconstruction work. Contractors' interest in avoiding the tax ran directly against taxpayers who funded the contracts.
